primary_meaning: “Year” has no single settled biblical symbolic meaning. When used figuratively or typologically, its broadest conventional association is a complete or divinely appointed season—especially a time of favor, judgment, release, or restoration.
primary_basis: Isaiah 61:1–2 and Luke 4:18–21 — “the year of the Lord’s favor” denotes the appointed era of salvation proclaimed and inaugurated by Christ.
Leviticus 25:8–13 — the Jubilee year provides the principal biblical pattern for release, restoration, liberty, and return.
Isaiah 34:8 and 63:4 — a “year” can mark an appointed period of divine vengeance or recompense.
Ecclesiastes 3:1 — supports the broader concept of divinely appointed times and seasons, though it does not assign a fixed symbolism to “year.”

alternatives.meaning: A literal calendar or regnal year with no symbolic significance. This is the ordinary meaning in most biblical occurrences.
A Jubilee-like era of salvation, liberation, forgiveness, and restoration.
An appointed period of divine judgment or recompense.

In prophetic interpretation, one symbolic day represents one literal year—the “day-year principle.” This is especially prominent in historicist interpretation but is not accepted as a universal rule across Christian traditions.
A standardized 360-day “prophetic year,” commonly inferred by correlating apocalyptic periods such as 1,260 days, 42 months, and “time, times, and half a time.”
A symbol of completeness simply because a year completes an annual cycle.

notes: Christian interpretation does not generally treat “year” as carrying one fixed symbolic value. Its meaning is determined by context: most occurrences are literal, while symbolic uses variously concern an appointed season, Jubilee restoration, judgment, or particular prophetic calculations.
